routes.description: Establish that belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God is irrational because the available evidence includes apparently gratuitous evil and confused salvation requirements, while the proposed arguments from reason, design, and morality do not adequately support that God.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the conflict between the claimed divine attributes and the observed world, together with epistemic and salvation confusion, defeats or outweighs the cumulative positive case for rational theism.

bridges.description: Given the available reason and evidence, belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God is irrational.

Apparently gratuitous evil and related epistemic confusion outweigh the proposed arguments for God and prevent those arguments from rationally supporting the all-powerful, all-loving God under discussion.
Pervasive suffering that appears to serve no greater good is improbable under an all-powerful, all-loving God, and merely possible theodicies do not make belief in that God rational.
An all-loving God would not attach grave eternal consequences to salvation conditions that sincere people cannot reliably identify and religious communities cannot agree upon.

Evolutionary accounts of cognition and morality, together with alternative explanations of apparent design, undercut the claim that reason, fine-tuning, or moral experience rationally identifies the proposed God.

routes.description: Establish that belief in God is rational through a cumulative case from the reliability of reason, the life-permitting structure of the universe, and objective morality, while answering the evidential challenge from suffering.
routes.successCriteria: Show that rationality, design, and morality are collectively more expected or intelligible if God exists than if God does not, and that suffering does not defeat this cumulative support.

bridges.description: The cumulative available evidence makes belief in God more rational than nonbelief.

The combined evidence from rational minds, cosmic design, and objective morality makes God more probable than God's nonexistence, while available responses prevent suffering from defeating that inference.
Unguided naturalism undermines confidence that evolved minds track truth, whereas an intelligent creator provides a rational basis for trusting human reason and the universe's intelligibility.
The universe's highly specific life-permitting conditions are substantially more probable under intelligent design than under an unguided chance hypothesis.
Objective moral obligations are difficult to ground in an impersonal, purposeless universe but are intelligible when goodness is grounded in God.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: A belief is rational when it accords with the reason and evidence available to the believer; rationality and truth are therefore distinct questions.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly hands the opening case to Stephen Woodford, and this passage continues his uninterrupted first-person definition of the debate's terms.
moves.selectionRationale: This 155-word opening passage presents one recoverable inferential framework through the miasma example and distinguishes rational belief from true belief. It is argumentative context rather than an introduction or logistical remark, but the standard itself does not yet supply a reason for or against any particular route bridge.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: The world appears filled with suffering that serves no greater good, while belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God requires denying that any such gratuitous evil exists.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Woodford's uninterrupted opening case and expresses the problem-of-evil position uniquely associated with his stated side.
moves.selectionRationale: This 115-word span isolates Woodford's core inference from observed mass extinctions, disasters, predation, disease, and suffering to tension with the asserted divine attributes. The span is bounded, participant-authored, and has a single role: presenting apparent gratuitous evil as evidence against the proposed God.

moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: If minds result only from mindless, unguided physical processes, confidence in their truth-tracking is self-undermining, whereas an intelligent creator explains why minds and the universe are intelligible.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator has explicitly handed the second opening case to Simon Edwards, and the passage continues his uninterrupted presentation of the argument from reason.
moves.selectionRationale: This 122-word span contains the complete contrast between the alleged self-defeat of atheistic naturalism and the theistic explanation of trustworthy intelligence. It is a bounded statement of one inferential role rather than a collection of the later design and morality arguments.

moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: The arguments from rationality, design, and morality cumulatively make God's existence more probable than God's nonexistence and therefore make belief in God more rational than the alternative.
moves.attributionBasis: This is the explicit conclusion of Edwards's uninterrupted opening case, immediately before the moderator thanks him and the audience applauds.
moves.selectionRationale: This 78-word conclusion expressly aggregates Edwards's three arguments and states the complete motion-level result. The bounded span has one function—drawing the cumulative inference to rational theism—and does not depend on moderator summary or audience adoption.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Evolution need not make cognition wholly unreliable because false representations are often costly, so selection can favor broadly accurate beliefs even though human access to truth remains imperfect.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Woodford, Edwards poses a question to him, and this passage begins Woodford's direct first-person answer before Edwards resumes.
moves.selectionRationale: This 143-word response isolates Woodford's evolutionary objection to the premise that unguided evolution deprives people of reason to trust cognition. Its single role is to argue that survival and broadly accurate representation commonly align while allowing ordinary cognitive error.

moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: Assessing earthly suffering must include an eternal future in which God has resources to redeem present suffering and wipe away people's tears.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the problem-of-evil question to Edwards, and the passage continues Edwards's uninterrupted first-person response from a Christian perspective.
moves.selectionRationale: This 99-word span isolates one response to the inference that observed suffering is gratuitous: the relevant accounting is not limited to earthly life because an afterlife permits divine redemption. It is distinct from Edwards's subsequent references to free will, soul-making, and divine participation in suffering.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Even granting arguments for a creator, the conflict between an all-powerful, all-loving God and the world's suffering prevents identifying that creator with the Christian God or Allah.
moves.attributionBasis: The surrounding exchange explicitly gives Woodford the response, and the first-person reference to his opening problem-of-evil case confirms the attribution.
moves.selectionRationale: This 162-word passage states Woodford's overarching inferential priority: positive creator arguments may be granted without overcoming the contradiction he alleges between the relevant divine attributes and the world. The span therefore captures a central route-level synthesis rather than another list of suffering examples.

moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: Whether biblical stories are real depends on literary genre: some books present historical records, while parables such as the Good Samaritan and prodigal son communicate truths without describing actual events.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the audience's Bible question to Edwards first, and the passage is his uninterrupted answer before Woodford is invited to respond.
moves.selectionRationale: This 129-word fourth-quartile passage offers an argumentative genre distinction concerning biblical narratives. It is a participant's substantive response rather than an audience assertion, but its proposition about history, poetry, and parable can remain true without changing the credibility of any stated route bridge.
